I have marked speaking exams for nine years, and the candidates who surprise me are almost never the ones with the widest vocabulary. They are the ones who do not stop. A short answer is not penalised for being short, exactly; it is penalised because there is nothing in it to assess. Eight words gives me no complex sentence, no linking, no evidence that you can develop an idea, so I have nothing to award marks for even when every word is right. What I tell people to practise is boring and it works. Answer the question. Then say why, or give one example. Then say what follows from it. Three sentences, roughly forty seconds, and you have shown me everything the criteria ask about. The candidates who do that are not more fluent than the others. They just decided in advance that they were going to say three things.

There is a particular thing that happens in meetings and almost nobody names it. Somebody answers a question accurately and stops, and the room moves on, and six months later that person is surprised not to be in the smaller meeting. It is not about confidence and it is not about English. It is that an answer with only one sentence in it gives the room nothing to build on. The people who get invited back are the ones who add the second thing: here is why, or here is an example, or here is what worries me about it. In fairness, some cultures train you out of that — saying more than you were asked can read as showing off, and I understand why people hold back. But in an American meeting the second sentence is where you exist. Say the thing you assumed was obvious. It usually is not.

The question is asked: how is the American operation going? The answer comes first, in one short sentence: slower than planned. A reason or an example follows: the bank account alone took four months. A point against the speaker is conceded: in fairness, nobody had seen that structure before. And the consequence closes it: the upshot is that nothing can be signed until the cap is agreed.
